Females of Andalusian barbel (Luciobarbus sclateri) exhibit a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 18% [GSI = 18%] during the prespawning period when water temperatures reach 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This relatively modest index suggests that ovarian investment, while substantial, is partitioned across multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season, a strategy common among iteroparous cyprinids inhabiting hydrologically variable environments. Field studies have further documented that vitellogenesis accelerates markedly once temperatures rise above 12 °C, with peak ovarian development occurring shortly before the late spring spawning migration. These data underscore the tight coupling between thermal cues and reproductive preparation in this species.

Growth trajectory analyses based on extensive mark-recapture records indicate that the ultimate total length achieved by this species is approximately 41.3 cm [Li = approximately 41.3 cm], a value that represents the asymptotic size predicted by von Bertalanffy growth models fitted to long-term monitoring data from the Guadiana River basin. This maximum recorded length is consistent with the upper size range reported for other large-bodied Luciobarbus species, though individuals rarely attain this dimension in heavily regulated river sections where habitat fragmentation and reduced flow regimes constrain somatic growth. The growth coefficient is relatively slow, reflecting the temperate climate and seasonal food availability that characterize the species' natural distribution. Larger specimens, those exceeding 35 cm, are typically found in deeper pool habitats with abundant cover, where they can exploit benthic macroinvertebrate prey without the energetic costs associated with maintaining position in fast-flowing riffles. Such habitat preferences likely contribute to the attainment of the ultimate length observed in undisturbed populations.

Sexual maturation in female Andalusian barbel begins when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 13.5 cm [Lp = 13.5 cm], though some variation exists across populations, with estimates ranging from 11 to 16 cm depending on local growth conditions and density-dependent factors. This length-based threshold is a reliable predictor of reproductive status, as gonadal histology confirms the onset of active oogenesis once females surpass this size. The relationship between body length and maturity is crucial for fisheries management, allowing managers to establish size limits that protect immature individuals from harvest. In practice, the length at first maturity serves as a conservative benchmark for minimum capture sizes, ensuring that most females have the opportunity to spawn at least once before entering the fishery. Comparable values have been reported for congeneric species inhabiting similar Mediterranean climates, suggesting a conserved evolutionary pattern linking body size with reproductive development in this genus.

Egg diameter measurements from gravid females captured during the spawning season average approximately 1.7 mm, which translates into a wet weight at birth for the newly hatched larvae of about 0.0026 g [Wwb = about 0.0026 g]. This modest larval mass reflects the relatively small, yolk-rich eggs typical of cyprinids that scatter their demersal eggs over gravel substrates, where the developing embryos rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. The small size at hatching imposes constraints on early life survival, as newly emerged larvae must rapidly locate suitable zooplankton prey within the first few days post-hatching to avoid starvation. Larvae of this mass are particularly vulnerable to predation from macroinvertebrates and small fishes, and their survival is strongly influenced by the timing of hatching relative to spring zooplankton blooms. Field observations indicate that larval abundance peaks approximately two weeks after the main spawning pulse, coinciding with elevated densities of rotifers and copepod nauplii in the riverine drift.

Longevity data derived from otolith readings of specimens collected across multiple river basins indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 6,570 days [am = approximately 6,570 days] under an average annual water temperature regime of 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C]. This extended lifespan, corresponding to roughly 18 years, places L. sclateri among the longer-lived Iberian freshwater fishes, a trait that confers demographic resilience in the face of environmental stochasticity. The slow growth rate and delayed maturation observed in this species are life-history correlates of this extended longevity, as individuals allocate resources to somatic maintenance and survival rather than to early reproduction. At the growth temperatures typical of this cyprinid's habitat, which average 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], females attain puberty at approximately 1,825 days [tp = approximately 1,825 days], or roughly five years of age, when they first become capable of contributing to the next generation. This combination of substantial longevity and delayed maturation suggests that population persistence depends heavily on the survival of older, larger females, which disproportionately contribute to recruitment through their higher fecundity and extended spawning seasons.
